prize_parts.citation: for a visionary body of work in Romanian, rooted in poetry and culminating in vast prose cycles, in which memory, the body and metaphysical speculation are built into a densely patterned imaginative architecture

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: one prize part, Cărtărescu alone. The case I can defend rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic ambition, and imaginative depth sustained at large scale, judged from public knowledge and translation, not from verified reading. The chair asked how to scrutinise a unanimous opening. I tried to build the best case against him and compared it with each rival. The rivals' cases are real but each is limited on at least one criterion. Michon has concentration but a slim corpus, and his effect depends on French syntax and cadence. Carson has formal invention, but the scope of the oeuvre is hard to fix. Can Xue has a rigorous method, but I cannot judge her development from a partial translated selection. Zurita has ambition, but the language on the page is hard to separate from the memorial project. On the chair's question about scope, I now favour a citation that follows the Olsson and Palm formulation. The evidential weight rests on the major prose cycles, namely the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, with the poetry named as the lyric root and not as an independently evidenced pillar. That wording is accurate about what the committee can actually assess, and it still describes a whole-oeuvre achievement attributable to one writer. If I had to test the widening-versus-repetition question against one comparison, it would be the later large novel against the Blinding trilogy: does it reorganise the material into a new form, or only re-run its motifs? I cannot settle that from reputation, so I treat it as the main open point and not as a point in his favour. Agreement among colleagues is not an argument and I give it no weight.
statement.case_against: I will argue the strongest case against, since the chair asked who would. The achievement is tied to dense Romanian patterning, wordplay and rhythm, and a committee reading in translation may be rewarding the translators' prose and the recognisable architecture of the books while missing the language. The very large scale and recurrent motifs may be insularity rather than deepening, and the long books may be uneven in control. The poetry and early work are thinner in translation, so a whole-oeuvre claim is weaker than a claim for the major novels. No member, including me, has direct command of the originals or has verified the texts. If the committee judged that translation obscures too much, the principled fallback would be a writer whose corpus can be assessed on firmer ground, and I would not force the Cărtărescu case through on reputation or on the unanimity of the openings.

responses.point: Palm argues that Cărtărescu's effect depends more on large-scale architecture and imagery, which survive translation better, than Michon's depends on syntax and cadence. She also acknowledges that the poetry and early work are unevenly translated.
responses.response: I accept the distinction as a judgment about the type of effect, and it is the strongest answer I have heard to the translation worry. Large-scale structure and recurrent imagery are more likely to carry over than cadence. But it only partly answers the concern, because what carries over may be the architecture and not the language, and the criteria also ask about linguistic achievement. I would therefore say plainly in the citation discussion that the case is stronger for the structure and imaginative design of the prose than for the sentence-level texture. I also agree with her on the poetry, and it is why I now favour a citation grounded in the prose with the poetry as the lyric root.

responses.point: Olsson says the repetition concern is the real test of this candidacy and must be answered from the books, not their reputation. He suggests a citation grounded mainly in the major prose, with poetry as a related strand, and keeps Carson as the English-language alternative if translation proves too weak a basis.
responses.response: I take up both points. I adopt his scope: the citation names the poetry as the root, but the weight falls on the prose cycles. On Carson as the fallback, I agree that her English-language corpus avoids the translation problem that weighs on Cărtărescu, which is a genuine point in her favour. The difficulty I named in round 1 remains, that a citation must say exactly what is honoured. I would limit it to renewal of the lyric and essayistic forms through her poetry and hybrid books, and set aside her translations and scholarship. That seems possible, so she stays as my first alternative. It is a narrower and less continuous case than the Cărtărescu one, and I would not move her above him on the evidence now available.

responses.point: Mattson reads motif recurrence across the large works as the means by which the project accumulates meaning, and she weighs Michon's recognisable voice more favourably than I did. She asks me to say more about how Carson's oeuvre could be fixed in a citation.
responses.response: On Michon, she has moved me somewhat. I ranked him seventh because of corpus size and translation loss, and I would not defend that placement as a verdict on the quality of his sentences. A concentrated oeuvre can meet the standard, and I accept that someone weighing intensity over scale could reasonably place him higher. My reservation is evidential and not aesthetic: a slim corpus gives less evidence of development, and the loss in translation is probably heaviest for his style. I therefore do not move him into my alternatives. On motif recurrence, I agree it can be accumulation, but the same observation fits a closed circuit, and only specific books can tell the two apart. I would not treat recurrence as evidence for either reading. On Carson, I answered her question to Olsson above: a lyric and essayistic-renewal scope.

responses.point: Sward holds that Can Xue's dream-logic method is a deliberate, rigorous strangeness with few parallels. She concedes that only part of the corpus is translated and that she cannot say whether the method deepens or repeats.
responses.response: We are in the same position on the evidence. I did not rank Can Xue in my top eight, and I do not read that as a verdict on the work, only on what I can assess. I find Sward's candour about the coverage gap persuasive. It is the reason I cannot treat her as an alternative to Cărtărescu in this vote, and I would not want it read as a rejection. If the committee could obtain a regional expert's account of how the later books differ from the earlier ones, I would revisit her ranking in a future round.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's dense Romanian patterning, wordplay and rhythm reaches the committee in translation, and whether the poetry and early work are covered well enough in translation to support more than a supporting role in the citation.

Whether recurrent motifs and the very large scale of the later novels amount to deepening or to self-repetition. This cannot be settled by reputation, and I have not independently verified any text or claimed to have read the originals.

Whether Carson's hybrid, partly object-based work can be framed as an oeuvre under Nobel's will without relying on translation or scholarship. I think a lyric and essayistic scope is possible but have not tested it.
For Yan Lianke, my other alternative, how to separate the effects of translation and censorship context from the literary assessment, and how uniform the quality is across a very large output.
My own voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the record does not show how it would count toward a four-vote majority.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict apparent from the supplied profile; I have no documented tie to any shortlisted writer. My own work is non-fiction and biography, which is context and not evidence of preference. I record that, as a co-opted member and Permanent Secretary, I carry a procedural role in announcing the outcome, which should not be confused with a literary preference for any candidate.
